Uniform Title: *Prodgītāgama* Main Title: *Prodgītāgamaḥ vivāhavidhimātram* Manuscript: IFP/EFEO Transcript T0201
Description: Transcribed from IFP transcript T0201, which was copied from a manuscript belonging to Swaminatha Gurukkal of Tiruvavadudurai.
For bibliographic details, see the Muktabodha IFP/EFEO online catalog at www.muktabodha.org.

|| Salutations to Śiva and Śivā. ||
When the [preliminary] song has been sung aloud, the marriage rite [commences].
Extremely delighted, Viṣṇu, with supreme devotion, questioned Śrīkaṇṭha Rudra, the Lord Īśāna, who is the ultimate refuge five times over.
O Blessed One, Lord of all the worlds, you who bear the burden of protecting the world;
at this time born of separation from Satī, the prosperity of the worlds has increased from the very beginning. (2)
O Soul of the Universe, it is said that at that time nothing existed; how then did the worlds remain?
And how did their uninterrupted origination come to be? (3)
"I do not know that secret; tell it to me, O ocean of compassion.
Thus was Mahādeva questioned by the powerful Viṣṇu.
The Lord of Pārvatī spoke to him, recounting the event:
"In ancient times, it is said, Dakṣa proceeded with a sacrifice that was devoid of the Lord."
Although you already know all this, nevertheless, out of regard for you, I shall relate it all; listen to the story in detail.
When Satī released her own body through meditative absorption,
the world then became devoid of festival and bereft of the increase of progeny.
Scorched by drought, it met with destruction day by day;
then the gods, led by Brahmā, assembled in my presence.
Having prostrated, he informed you of the world's great distress;
then, O Acyuta, for the sake of the welfare of the world, you awakened him.
O Lord of the Earth, the lineage of Indra and the other guardians of the quarters shall flourish there; even in that place, she shall become Gaurī, who is unborn.
When he himself gave that maiden to Vāmadeva, who is Śiva, from that time onwards, it is said, this world began to flourish as before. (11)
Thus commanded, those gods performed the marriage rites for the two of them;
I shall describe that, so listen with due respect. (12)
Then the four-faced Brahmā, the lords of sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others, appeared together with their wives, desiring to do what was pleasing to Maheśa.
For the sake of winning over the world, they adopted a worldly course of conduct and dispatched the Seven Sages for the purpose of deciding upon the maiden.
Accompanied by their wives, they arrived at the supreme palace of the lord of mountains,
which was provided with coconut, plantain, and betel-nut trees.
Taking a pair of garments and a bodice adorned with gold,
they joyfully chose the maiden who was seated upon the lap of the Lord of Mountains.
Her face possessed the luster of the full moon, her hair was dark and curled,
and she was graced by the makara-bannered god of love arising from the corners of her beautiful smiles.
Then, accompanied by the chanting of the Veda (brahmaghoṣa) with the mantra "uduttara," Arundhatī honored the girl with offerings of fragrant flowers.
He adorned the well-pleased Umā, who was herself beautifully decorated;
then, filled with wonder, Himavat gazed upon Menakā’s face.
Then the goddess consented to give the mountain to Maheśa, who was in the form of Śambhu; at that time, the lord of the earth was also present with her. (20)
Then that lord of mountains spoke these words: "I shall give [it].
This was said when the lord of medicinal herbs had attained full growth and was in a state of great abundance.
On a lunar day associated with the Jāmitra yoga, during the Maitra muhūrta, under the moon,
and conjoined with the Uttaraphalgunī nakṣatra, they fixed the auspicious moment.
Thus, "cause the marriage to be performed according to the path taught in the scriptures," said the wielder of the Pināka bow, Maheśvara, and dispatched Brahmā.
In that very manner, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, caused it to be performed;
and by this same rite, the Mountain gave Pārvatī in marriage.
For this very reason, the lineage of the gods did not flourish;
even for Indra, there was only Jayanta and Nalakūbara.
He indeed became the progeny of Kubera among the gods;
though bodiless, he then became possessed of limbs, the lord who brings delight to Rati.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Marriage," as it was proclaimed.
Then Viṣṇu, with supreme joy, questioned Mahādeva:
"There is dissolution in the world of men; there is the destruction of creatures at every step. (1)
"O Lord, tell me how poverty and hatred toward living beings might not occur.
Then Mahādeva spoke regarding the marriage rite of Gaurī.

In the sanctuary and in the installation, especially during festivals and other such occasions, the rite must be performed according to the prescribed rules, in accordance with the injunctions of the Vedas and the Āgamas. || 3 ||
I shall speak of that; listen, O Viṣṇu, O Janārdana, in brief.
This [teaching] bestows long life and health, and increases one's sons and grandsons.
Grain brings fame and wards off untimely death;
it always bestows auspiciousness and, in particular, increases happiness.
In the months of Phālguna, Caitra, or Vaiśākha, or especially under the Tiṣya asterism,
or under Uttaraphalgunī, Anurādhā, or other auspicious constellations.
During the auspicious muhūrtas on a day of the planet Venus,
the practitioner who is learned in all tantras should perform the marriage rite.
He is consecrated by the twice-born of Śiva;
he is a knower of the investigation of the Śiva-śāstras and is proficient in the Śiva-āgamas.
Wearing a *dukūla* garment as an upper cloth, his body was adorned with ashes and a rosary of *rudrākṣa* beads. || 9 ||
He was adorned with a golden sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*),
his limbs were smeared with white sandalwood paste, and he was decorated with white garlands.
Thus, having performed the vow according to its characteristics, one should pray to the God of gods: "O Guru, grant me prosperity! || 11 ||
Having thus prayed and paid homage,
the preceptor [should act] after the sacrificer has likewise made this earnest petition. (12)
In a beautiful assembly pavilion provided with a hundred pillars,
adorned with plantain trunks, date palms, canopies, banners, arches, flags, and incense, it was made resplendent. || 14 ||
Amidst the sounding of various musical instruments such as paṇavas and maddalas,
within a bright pavilion adorned [with jewels], [the Brahmins] were present;
and there were kings, ministers, soldiers, and warriors.
In the center of the decorated hall, one should respectfully construct a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*);
in its middle, a lotus-altar (*padmavedī*), and to its east, a lotus-pit (*padmakuṇḍa*).
One should construct a svastika mandala according to the procedure taught in the Āgamas;
and upon a noble throne in the western quarter, which is called the svastika, one should [worship] Maheśvara.
Having established Gaurī, who possesses an auspicious form, on the right side,
he should place Himavat along with Menakā on the right-hand side of the Goddess.
One should worship Viṣṇu, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, in the water-pots;
and on the southern side of the fire, Vāgdevī and the Four-faced One (Brahmā).
One should worship Sanaka and the other lords of yogis in front of Brahmā;
and on the left side of the deity, one should worship Durgā and the other Yoginīs.
In the north-eastern direction of the Lord, [he should worship] the Rudras, the leaders of the Pramathas,
the seven sages (Saptarṣis) along with their wives, and the entire circle of divine sages (Devarṣis).
One should worship Śacī, Indra, and the Vasus in the eastern part;
and in the western part, one should worship Menakā and the other hosts of Apsarases.
One should worship Viṣṇu and the other hosts of deities in the pitchers according to their sequence, and in the images according to the procedure of the Miśra-tantra.
In the presence of the God of gods, together with the image-makers, the preceptor should formally grant permission in an assembly of Brahmins according to the prescribed rite.
O God of gods, Lord of the world, cause of the world’s joy!
For the sake of auspiciousness and for the welfare of the world, I have set out.
"O Lord, grant me your command for the sake of the desired objects of the worlds.
Then, having gone to the temple of the Goddess, one should pray for the attainment of one's desired goal. (28)
O Ambikā, O Goddess, O auspicious one, O moonlight that is a mine of compassion, you shall become the consort of Śambhu for the sake of destroying the afflictions of the world. (29)
Having spoken thus to that Great Goddess and prostrated before her, the supreme preceptor assumes the form of the marriage deity and prays for the attainment of his desired goal.
Among the gods beginning with Somāskanda and those consisting of twenty-five, according to the ritual procedure for whichever one among them is endowed with Śakti.
Every year, one should perform the most excellent wedding ceremony;
for the sake of the intention of marriage, one should worship the two Gods of gods. (32)
Having worshipped Śakti and Vighneśa, preceded by the propitiation of the planets,
one should then perform the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) for the collection of clay and the rite of sprouting seeds (aṅkura).
Having prepared and tied the protective amulet for both the Goddess and the God,
he should rise early the next morning and then gather the necessary ritual materials.
Then, having gone to the temple of the Goddess, one should perform the rite for the determination of speech.
Thereafter, the gods beginning with Brahmā and the lords of sages beginning with Vasiṣṭha [arrived].
Desiring to please Maheśa and for the sake of gathering the world together, they appeared accompanied by their wives, having adopted a worldly mode of life.
Having worshipped the gods and others with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth,
[he should offer] together with coconuts, plantains, and betel nuts.
Having taken up a pair of garments and a bodice adorned with gold, [he should do so] with the mantra "uduttara" preceded by the chanting of the Vedas (brahmaghoṣa). 38.
Having made his request and worshipped the Goddess with offerings of garments and flowers,
he then especially propitiated the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) for the sake of marriage.
Having performed the worship of the previous day with water mixed with the aforementioned substances for the feet,
mouth-rinsing, and the arghya offering, one should enter the bathing hall.
Having established him upon the lion-throne accompanied by dance and song,
[one should perform] an anointing with fragrant oil, as well as bathing and the application of unguents.
One should perform bathing with warm water and consecration with all [auspicious] substances;
thereafter, one should especially carry out the wiping with a clean cloth. (42)
He wears a lower garment of fine linen and is provided with an upper garment;
he is anointed with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, saffron, and other unguents. || 43 ||
Having offered incense made from agaru wood for the hair according to the prescribed rite,
one should likewise offer jasmine, mālatī, jāti, campaka, and other flowers.
She wears a crown of nine jewels and has the crescent moon as her ear-ornament;
there is vermilion at the parting of her hair and likewise a tilaka mark upon her forehead.
Having placed below the black collyrium, the pair of ear-lobes, the pair of jeweled earrings, and also the nose ornament; 46.
In the lower [region], there is indeed Yāvaka, and then Prathamabhūṣaṇa;
likewise Cintāka, Pataka, and Mahāpataka. || 47 ||
One may designate a single string of pearls as a *muktāvalī*,
or even as a *vaikakṣya* necklace, or likewise as a *hāra* consisting of four armlets.
Having placed rows of bracelets, as well as a series of rings, and having fastened a girdle-string and then a waist-cord above it; (49)
The "Ornament of Good Fortune" (Saubhāgyābharaṇa), adorned with all kinds of jewels, as well as bracelets for the feet and jeweled anklets; || 50 ||
Having especially placed a ring upon his foot, and having taken various weapons in his hand according to the specific requirements of each occasion; || 51 ||
(9) One should perform the mounting of the sandals accompanied by great auspicious rites;
having likewise offered incense and lamps, one should then present the five kinds of food.
Having worshipped Gaurī, who possesses an auspicious form, with the sixteen types of offerings and betel-leaf accompanied by sacred flowers, using their respective mantras; (53)
Then, having mounted the goddess— thoroughly adorned— upon an elephant or a lion,
[he should proceed] to the banks of rivers or to water-stations for the sake of worshiping Ādiśakti.
Then, having caused the Goddess to enter [the image] amidst the sounds of various musical instruments,
he should duly place the water-pot and worship it with the ritual offerings.
With great care, she adorned him with applications of musk and saffron, collyrium and the like, and with most beautiful ornaments such as earrings, eyes, and mirrors. || 56 ||
Having offered seeds and mung beans as the sacrificial food (naivedya), one should perform the concluding rite (pūrṇakarma);
one should offer praise together with Brahmins who are knowers of the Veda and are facing the east.
I bow to the Great Goddess, the Mahātripurabhairavī, who is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and whose form is immeasurable.
"O Goddess, my chosen deity, O Goddess who increases my joy, I choose as my husband a Śiva who is exceedingly beautiful. (59)
"O Mother of the World, bring about [this] for the increase of long-lasting auspiciousness!
Having thus prayed to the Supreme Goddess and worshipped her thereafter— || 60 ||
Having meditated upon that immeasurable Primordial Power (Ādi-śakti), he attained a state of immovability;
right there, he should diligently perform the birth rites and other ceremonies for the Goddess.

(10) The preceptor, preceded by the sound of musical instruments, taking up all the ritual requisites for the auspicious and other rites of the God of gods, [should proceed] toward the various forms. 62.
Having gone before anyone at all and made his request while standing in front of them:
"O God of gods, Lord of the world, O Master who removes the suffering of the world! (63)
"O Lord, grant me your permission now for the sake of my welfare," having thus entreated the Lord of Gods and offered incense and lamps. (64)
Then, having performed the consecration with bathing powders and ablution waters, and having recited the Rudrādhyāya mantra, accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments; 65.
The crown, armlets, bracelets, necklace, anklets, and rings;
the waist-string, the sacred thread, and [the offering of] oblations. 66.
With these and other such items, as well as with sandals and the like, and with jasmine, campaka, punnāga, kahlāra, and * * * * [flowers]. (67)
One should cause [this] to be made for Śiva, the God of gods, the Supreme Self.
Then, having performed the vows and other auspicious rites,
and having worshipped Śiva with all ritual offerings, one should cause Him to mount the bull.
Equipped with all musical instruments and various [ornaments],
having gone there together with her, [he should honor her] with water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, and so forth.
Then, having performed the ritual service (*upacāra*), [one should perform] the fourfold [rite]. || 71 ||

Having performed the ritual services according to the scriptures with offerings of food, incense, lamps, umbrellas, and the fanning of yak-tail whisks, one should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Having raised it, one should place it in front of the pavilion, facing east and west.
And having exchanged garlands, and having circumambulated [the deity] with musical instruments accompanied by female attendants and lamps; || 74 ||
Having seated them facing the east in the beautiful Kalyāṇamaṇḍapa and the Svastimaṇḍapa, they remained there.
Then the preceptor, together with the practitioners, should perform the offering to the yakṣas;
[therein] the auspicious plantain fruit [is offered].
The wise one should offer a bali-oblation accompanied by red flowers;
having made the formal resolve for the marriage, he should send forth the bridegroom.
And the worship of the gods, such as Hari and Brahmā, [should be performed] with water-pots. || 78 ||
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the sacrifice with the appropriate ritual;
one should carry out the dispatching of the boon (*varapreṣaṇa*) with the mantra beginning "prasugman."
With the mantra beginning "āpaḥ...," he should offer water for the feet;
with the mantra "yanmadhuno madhavya," he should present the honey-mixture (madhuparka). || 80 ||
p.
12) Having performed the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) for the giving of the maiden according to the prescribed rule therein, and having taken [the bride]... indeed [attaining] Śiva. || 81 ||
One should perform the grasping of the hand with the mantra beginning "gṛbhṇāmi," and then [proceed] with a concealed garment... || 82 ||
Having taken that pair of garments, he placed them upon it according to the prescribed rite.
The preceptor, having tied an auspicious thread with the seed-mantra of Gaurī, should bestow grace upon me. 84.
The best of men, [holding] the sandals of Pārvatī, should proceed seven times in succession with the mantra "ekamiṣe. (85)
Having established the Śiva-fire preceded by the ritual strewing of grass,
one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with the root mantra and with the mantra "Somāya," followed by the offering of parched grain (*lājahoma*) while circumambulating to the right.

Having performed this three times over the kindled fire, one should offer the remaining oblations of clarified butter with the mantras beginning with "cittaṃ ca cetyaṃ" and the Jaya and other offerings.
It was provided with groups of fruits such as coconut and wood-apple,
and accompanied by grapes, dates, oranges, sugar-candy, and granulated sugar.
Adorned with pieces of sugarcane,
he then offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) while reciting the mantra beginning with "sapta" seven times.
Having performed the service of attendance, one should prostrate...
[and] having placed moist unbroken grains [upon it], the recitation of auspicious blessings (*svastivācana*) should be performed.
With offerings such as incense, lamps, food-oblations, and betel-leaf, and having previously offered cakes and sweetmeats... 93.
Then, having offered betel-leaf and other items, as well as perfumes, flowers, and so forth,
he should perform a circumambulation of the street for the sake of bestowing grace upon all.
He shall obtain long life and find sons and grandsons.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Marriage," as it was proclaimed. || 26 ||
